title: Otherworldly Adventures: The many spectral encounters of local historian, ghost researcher Richard Senate
site_name: VC Reporter | Times Media Group - News, Culture, Arts and Opinion
excerpt: Richard Senate has hunted ghosts for most of his life. The first one he ever saw was when he was a young man working on an archeological project at Mission
content:
Richard Senate has hunted ghosts for most of his life. The first one he ever saw was when he was a young man working on an archeological project at Mission San Antonio de Padua, founded by Junípero Serra in 1771 and located at U.S. Army Fort Hunter Liggett in Monterey County.

The Ventura historian and author — now one of California’s best-known paranormal investigators — was living among friars on the mission grounds during 1978. Late one night, he walked across the beautiful courtyard with its fountain and rose garden to enjoy a midnight snack from the kitchen where he had been washing dishes earlier that day. Senate noticed a dim light in the darkness and believed he saw a monk wearing a hood and carrying a candle in his hand.

“Well, did that scare me? No. It’s a monastery. Monks live there. So, I got to the very center of the courtyard and I decided, instead of going that way to the kitchen, I would go this way and find out who my fellow night owl was. That one decision changed my life,” Senate told a rapt audience during an Aug. 27 talk at Ventura’s Avenue Library. 

Senate approached the figure from the back and never saw a face. 

“I could see the folds of his garment in the moonlight. So, I’m getting up, I get about 10 feet, and then all of a sudden, he’s gone! He just disappeared! He didn’t fade away. He didn't swirl around and sparkle like “Star Trek” beaming up. He just wasn’t there anymore.”

Senate’s mouth dropped wide open and his first thought was that the monk fell in a hole so Senate looked around to see if the man needed help. 

“Then I realized, well, maybe he blew out the candle and ran away just to freak me out. And then I realized we’re on gravel. If he did that, I would have heard him. Then I realized I heard my footsteps, but I never heard his. And that’s when it dawned on me. This must have been one of those ghosts they talk about,” Senate said. “By the way, I lost my appetite. I went back to my room and kept the light on all night long.” 

Brother Joseph

The next morning at breakfast, Senate asked the monks if they ever saw ghosts.

“They told me all sorts of tales of glowing balls of light, strange apparitions or some rooms that seemed to shake like an earthquake, but there was nothing there. The weirdest story of all, the headless horsewoman would ride around the mission at night,” said Senate.

Then he described another tale the monks told him which seemed to fit in with the ghost he encountered. The story involved a long-ago member of the Franciscan order who was beloved for his kindness and who people thought of like a living saint, Brother Joseph. 

“Every night, Brother Joseph would get up at 12:30, light a candle and go from his room into the church to pray for an extra hour. And after his death — he’s buried there — they’d see him doing that. That’s what I saw. I didn’t know the story but I encountered Brother Joseph and that’s what did it. From that day on I wanted to find out what ghosts were.” 

Adventures with the paranormal

Senate’s encounter with the ghostly monk inspired him to start researching ghosts in Ventura County. He quickly heard about 25 or 30 haunted locations. Decades later, he has investigated thousands of reports. Senate has written numerous books and articles about ghosts and produced a cable-access TV show in Ventura for many years called “Ghost Hunters.”

Senate’s local fame attracted the attention of other ghost hunters including Zak Bagans, known for the hit TV show “Ghost Adventures,” who featured Senate in an episode about La Purísima Mission State Historic Park near Lompoc.

Senate had spent more than two years researching the site which he describes as the most haunted California mission, because it’s an actual battleground, locations which he explained are almost always haunted. In 1824, Indigenous people rose up against the rule of the Spanish, captured some Spanish cannons and mounted them on the mission walls.

“When the Spanish came, they were a little astounded. They shot a cannon at them and they fired back. And there was a big bloody battle that took place at that particular site,” the historian explained.

Strange things happened when Senate accompanied Bagans to the site.

“By the way, Zak is just as crazy in real life as he is on TV. But he was astounded. I was leading him around the haunted site. We went up to the padre’s bedroom and all of their equipment went dead. All the batteries drained. And they started to freak out. It was really weird,” Senate recalled.  

Other haunted locations Senate shared stories about included The Glen Tavern Inn in Santa Paula, Ventura’s Olivas Adobe, Port Hueneme’s Bard Mansion, Ojai’s Creek Road, the Petit House at Oxnard’s Heritage Square and Mission Basilica San Buenaventura. Senate suggested aspiring ghost hunters also head south to RMS Queen Mary ocean liner in Long Beach and the Whaley House in San Diego, two of California’s most haunted sites.

During a question-and-answer period following Senate’s talk, a woman brought up a city-sponsored ghost tour Senate guided many years ago at Olivas Adobe where she and about 14 others saw a ghostly girl in the children’s room wearing an old-fashioned nightgown, who dissipated as they approached. She described a coldness in the room but said her camera became hot and didn’t work anymore. She called it an experience she will never forget.

“We had over a hundred people see that little girl,” Senate responded. “For up to a year, she kept appearing. She was the greatest ghost of all! Just saying her name, Maria, then she’d come. And people accused me of having a projector or something…And then all of a sudden, she stopped coming. I think she’s still there but she’s just given up on making an appearance.”  

Long history of ghosts

Senate told his fans that ghosts are a topic worth studying as all human cultures have ghost stories. Theories include ghosts as projections of people’s minds or that people are seeing images of things that happened earlier in time.

“Some say there are demons that are disguised as ghosts, that’s a very popular belief, many religious groups have them. Now, is that true? Maybe. No one knows for certain. Many questions, a few answers, but is it well worth the study? Yes. It’s well worth trying to examine what these ghostly phenomena are,” he said.

Senate told aspiring ghost hunters to keep an open mind when investigating the paranormal. He’s seen things with his own eyes he could not explain, but thinks that someday people will have an answer 

“And someday, of course, we’ll all die. And on that day, maybe we’ll learn. I’d like to think that maybe I will. I’ll just keep investigating, but from the other side, and I’ll come back and tell you what I found,” Senate said. “Because I definitely believe that there’s more to it. And the more I’ve gotten into it, the more metaphysical I’ve become. And I now don’t fear death. I don’t believe that any of us really die. There is no death. We continue to live in another form, in another way.” 

Ghost Hunters Club

Senate’s talk at the Avenue Library also marked the launch of a new Ghost Hunters Club at the Westside branch of the Ventura County Library System.

Mary Birch is the Avenue Library branch manager and has been with the county’s library system since 2010. Birch told the VCReporter she had been thinking about starting a Ghost Hunters Club for some time. She had attended Senate’s ghost tours in the past and reached out for his advice.

“I asked him if he would like to present to kick off the Ghost Hunters Club, and here he is,” Birch said. “He does a great job, right?”

Birch said the Ghost Hunters Club will look into the history of ghosts and visit haunted sites. The library is also acquiring ghost hunting devices which can be checked out just like a library book so people can look for ghosts at their own homes or other sites.

“We’re gonna get that equipment so that we can go out and investigate,” Birch said. “We have a really good mentor. I think this is going to end up really successful.”

Birch expected about 25 or 30 people to show up for Senate’s talk; about 75 turned out. 

“It was huge,” Birch said. “I thought it would be decently attended, but I was really gratified how many people just thought this was so cool.” 

From Jungleland to TV

After the talk, Senate shared some details with the VCReporter about his life leading up to seeing his first ghost. His dad was a painter at MGM Studios but quit because he didn’t like the “factory element” of the job and started working for traveling carnivals, where the rides needed repainting. 

“He loved it because the boss gave him total rein and said just make it look pretty, whatever color,” Senate said. “I got to be his assistant whether I liked it or not. He never paid me anything.”

“I learned all about carnival life. I could short change people at the age of 6…it was a strange way to grow up really,” said Senate, who later worked with his dad at Jungleland in Thousand Oaks where he recalls painting the wagon wheels for movie props. 

The latest book Senate is working on is called “Strange New Sciences,” about pseudoscience, he said, where he writes about ghost tales, cryptozoology including Bigfoot hunters, and ancient records that indicate people were flying long before the invention of airplanes.

“There are a few that look like they might make it as a legitimate science,” Senate said of his findings. 

The book also covers astro-archeology and how the stars may have influenced ancient people to create structures designed to work with the various constellations or the moon, including Stonehenge in the United Kingdom. 

“It’s a really fascinating subject,” Senate said. “One of them is the Painted Cave (Chumash Painted Cave State Historic Park in the Santa Ynez mountains near Santa Barbara) which is a group of designs which seems to indicate an eclipse that happened in the 16th century. So, they evidently were recording these things.” 

‘Dark Tourism’ continues to grow

Senate said ghost hunting as a hobby is growing and that so-called “dark tourism” has become a multi-million-dollar industry. Museums have been created on the topic, including Zak Bagans’ The Haunted Museum in Las Vegas.

Senate said there are reasons to be skeptical of some claims, especially when people are charging money for a ghostly experience. He recalled being invited to attend a ghost tour in Virginia City, Nevada at the Washoe Club, a site from 1875 with a long history of being haunted. Senate was given a ticket for free while others were charged $1,500, he said. 

“I could see things that they were faking. They actually had a cutout of one of the characters from a horror movie,” he said.

Senate is frequently asked if he’s hoping to become a ghost after he dies.

“I have a whole list of people I’m going to haunt,” he replied. “There’s a lot of answers I want to get from the other side.”

After all his years of hunting ghosts, Senate said he has no fear of death, and has learned what it means to be alive.

“You’re here to improve yourself. That’s what it’s all about…To get through that lifetime and maybe learn something. A little tolerance maybe,” Senate said. “But I do think that I’ll find out when I die. And if I come back, maybe I’ll tell you.” 

“Ghostly Lore and Spirit Detecting with Richard Senate” will take place on Thursday, Oct. 29, 6-7 p.m. at the Avenue Library, 606 N. Ventura Avenue, Ventura. Learn more about this event and other programming at venturafriendsofthelibrary.org.
